title: How to Replace a Clogged Shower Valve: Cartridge Removal, Orientation, and Testing (This Old House)

locations.name: Basement shut-off (not behind the valve plate)
locations.basis: Transcript notes that there are no shut-offs behind the plate and the water shut-off is in the basement

summary: This Old House walks through diagnosing and replacing a clogged shower valve cartridge in a residential bath. The host explains how a pressure-balancing cartridge manages hot and cold water to prevent scalding, identifies common clog sources (impurities and rust), and demonstrates removing the faceplate, locating and extracting the cartridge with its retainer clip, inspecting for debris, installing a new cartridge with proper orientation (H and C marks) and lubrication on O-rings, and finally testing the shower to confirm hot and cold operation. The video also notes that rust from the building’s water supply can contaminate the cartridge, and emphasizes exercising the piston every 2-3 months to avoid sticking. A brief discussion about shut-off valves behind the plate and the basement shut-off is included, highlighting maintenance considerations for multi-unit buildings.
topics: Valve body anatomy (hot port, cold port, mixing cartridge)
Draining and water containment during service
Rust and sediment from steel-tank water supply
Exercise/maintenance of the pressure balance piston

sections.title: Valve anatomy and function
sections.description: Explanation of the shower valve's internal layout: hot water on one side, cold on the other, a cartridge that mixes water, and a pressure-balancing piston that adjusts for pressure changes to prevent scalding.

sections.title: Preparation and plate access
sections.description: The host notes the need to shut off water, explains that shut-offs behind the plate may not exist, and prepares by removing the plate while protecting the drain to prevent screws from escaping.

sections.title: Cartridge removal, inspection, and replacement
concepts: Identifying hot/cold ports and internal passages
Inspecting for dirt, rust, and debris
sections.description: The retainer clip is pulled, the cartridge is extracted, and the interior ports and pressure-balancing piston are inspected for impurities. A new cartridge is installed, with waterproof grease applied to O-rings and orientation verified by H and C marks.

sections.title: Reassembly, testing, and result
sections.description: The installer reseats the retainer clip, restores the water supply, and tests the shower to confirm both hot and cold water flow. The test demonstrates a successful valve repair and discusses the probable cause (piston clog from impurities) and the importance of exercising the piston periodically.

sections.title: Maintenance insights and diagnosis
sections.description: Explanation that impurities and rust can clog the pressure-balancing piston/cartridge, with a note that the piston can seize if not exercised every 2-3 months, along with a link to rust mechanisms from steel-tank water supplies.

sections.title: Shut-off considerations for service
concepts: Importance of accessible shut-offs in multi-unit buildings
sections.description: A brief discussion on the lack of shut-off valves behind the plate and the importance of having accessible shut-offs (especially in apartment buildings) for future service.

featured_techniques.technique: Identify and diagnose a clogged pressure-balancing cartridge by inspecting the internal cartridge for impurities and rust.
Replace a shower valve cartridge with orientation marks (H and C) and lubricate O-rings with waterproof grease before reinstalling.
Test the rebuilt valve by validating hot and cold water flow after reassembly to confirm proper operation.
Use a retainer clip and careful shielding to prevent water or debris from entering the wall during cartridge removal.
Explain and demonstrate the role of the pressure-balancing piston in preventing scalding during pressure fluctuations (e.g., toilet flush).
